title: Distributed Tracing
description: Master distributed tracing with W3C Trace Context, span trees, tail-based sampling, and learn how to debug N+1 queries across service boundaries using Jaeger.

segments.text: A user request hits your API gateway, which calls auth service, which calls user service, which queries the database. Latency is high. But which service is slow? Without distributed tracing, you're grep-ing through logs from fifty services trying to correlate timestamps. It's detective work without fingerprints.

W3C Trace Context standardizes how trace information propagates. Every request gets a trace ID — a unique 128-bit identifier. Each service operation creates a span with its own span ID. The traceparent header carries both: version, trace ID, parent span ID, and sampling flags.

Spans form a tree. The root span is the gateway request. It has child spans for each downstream call. Those child spans have their own children. The span tree shows exactly where time was spent — gateway took two milliseconds, auth took five, user-service took one hundred because it made forty database queries.

Jaeger, created at Uber, is the most widely used open-source tracing backend. Architecture: services report spans to the jaeger-agent sidecar, which batches and sends to jaeger-collector, which writes to storage — Elasticsearch or Cassandra. The UI lets you search by trace ID, service, or latency threshold.

At scale, you can't trace every request. Google processes billions of requests per second — storing every trace would cost millions. Head-based sampling decides at the start: trace one percent. But this misses rare errors. Tail-based sampling collects all spans, then decides after the request completes — keep all slow or errored traces.
Tail-based sampling sounds perfect, but it has a huge operational cost. Think about what infrastructure you'd need to buffer all spans before making a sampling decision.
segments.thought_prompt: What's the infrastructure cost of tail-based sampling? How would you handle the buffering?

segments.text: The killer use case: detecting N-plus-one queries across service boundaries. A product page calls inventory service once per product in the cart. Twenty items means twenty RPCs instead of one batched call. The span tree makes this painfully obvious — twenty identical child spans from one parent.

At Uber, tracing revealed a six-second latency spike on ride requests. The span tree showed the pricing service was calling a currency conversion API synchronously for each surge zone — forty sequential calls. One trace told the story that three weeks of log analysis hadn't uncovered. They switched to batched calls, latency dropped to two hundred milliseconds.

Trace-driven testing is an emerging practice. Record production traces, replay them in staging, and compare span trees. If the new version adds unexpected spans or increases latency on any span by more than twenty percent, the test fails. Netflix uses this to catch performance regressions before deployment.
You're designing tracing for a system with five hundred microservices processing one million requests per second. What sampling strategy, storage backend, and retention policy would you choose?
segments.thought_prompt: Design a tracing pipeline for 500 services at 1M req/sec. What are your sampling, storage, and retention decisions?

segments.text: Distributed tracing gives you X-ray vision into microservice architectures. Use W3C Trace Context for interoperability, tail-based sampling for capturing errors, and build dashboards that show p99 latency per span. The trace is the new stack trace — without it, debugging distributed systems is guesswork.
